We have 9 frontier models each judging the same 500 outputs — how should we combine their votes into a final score?
expected_behavior: warns that frontier judges share training data/alignment recipes so errors correlate, and a naive vote/average can carry far less independent signal than the raw judge count suggests
recommends measuring co-failure/agreement on the user's own eval set rather than assuming judge agreement equals correctness, and checking whether a single best judge already matches the panel

points to at least one concrete aggregation option beyond plain averaging (e.g. reliability/validation-weighted voting, geometric median for corruption-robustness, or judge-aware Bradley-Terry) matched to the situation
points to references/aggregation-methods.md for the fuller method-selection detail instead of inlining everything

cases.prompt: Our two LLM judges disagree on which response is better about 20% of the time — what should we do?
expected_behavior: treats disagreement as signal, not noise to average away — recommends surfacing/explaining it rather than silently collapsing to a majority
suggests a conditional escalation pattern (add a third judge, or route to a human) specifically on disagreement rather than always paying for N judges
does not suggest uncalibrated self-reported confidence as the fix

cases.prompt: Is it fine to have each judge state a confidence score and then average verdicts weighted by that confidence?
expected_behavior: flags that uncalibrated self-reported confidence adds little over plain majority vote and can be inversely correlated with correctness on hard items

recommends validating calibration first (e.g. against a human-labeled sample, Cohen's kappa / Krippendorff's alpha) before trusting confidence-weighting, or defaulting to historical-reliability weighting instead
does not present confidence-weighting as safe by default

cases.prompt: We're using an LLM judge to do pairwise comparisons between two model responses — anything we should watch out for?
expected_behavior: recommends running each pairwise comparison in both orders and only counting a win when both orders agree (else treat as a tie) to control position bias
notes the cost tradeoff of pairwise being O(n^2) and suggests pointwise scoring with periodic pairwise calibration at scale
mentions using a judge from a different model family than the generator to limit self-preference bias
